Vira Toland (Ostrey Hollow, recorded 1979) recounts how the 1919 Association letter accusing Ostrey Hollow milk haulers of watering their milk was actually caused by station tester Ansel Keddie skimming cream, which he was eventually caught and fired for—but the family rift it caused (Keddie's wife Orra estranged from her brother Emmet Brant) and the community's suspicion never fully healed.
This document is the 1966 annual report of the Pruett County Road Commission (recommending a levy for 1967, not 1908), so it contains no information about a road levy for 1908.

Effie Loomis (Association secretary 1901–1940, writing 1941) gives an institutional history of the Larrow Valley Creamery Association, centering on Article VII's rule that a station's own test is final, and on the 1925 arbitration that paid Ostrey Hollow patrons $3,800 while officially finding "no cause established"—while flagging the lost 1889–92 minutes and the unmentioned 1923 condemned measuring crate as gaps in the record.
The play being performed at the Ellerby Playhouse is *The Sparrow Hotel*.

Ansel Keddie (Ostrey Hollow tester), in his 1925 arbitration statement and an unsent letter, insists he tested milk scrupulously for 29 years and never skimmed cream, offering meticulous procedural detail and flagging an unexplained 1911 anomaly (tests jumped while using a borrowed measure) as the real mystery behind the chronic low readings—yet he was dismissed anyway despite the board finding "no cause established."
The wholesale order Elias Norcross placed with Purcell & Weare on 14 March 1932 totaled $59.65.

Ivy Keddie (Ansel Keddie's granddaughter), in a 1959 historical society talk, uses the rediscovered crate of condemned pipettes to prove the Ostrey Hollow station's chronically low butterfat readings were caused by a 5%-short measuring instrument—not watered milk or stolen cream—vindicating her grandfather decades after his 1925 dismissal.
Tamsin Ochoa's service number is 4471-K.

Wilbur Teague (Association bookkeeper, 1905–1945), writing in 1948, describes the "station gain" line he invented showing Ostrey Hollow's cream consistently arrived at Larrow Green heavier than what patrons were credited for, and argues this steady 5¼% gap reflects the structural opportunity for a lone tester to skim cream—implicitly supporting the embezzlement explanation rather than a mechanical fault.
Judge Thurlow Vane's court fined Delia Fought $5.00 for the petty theft of dress goods.

Merle Strawn (retired state dairy inspector), in his 1936 covering note and circuit-book extracts, presents his dry year-by-year inspection log of the Ordell circuit, notably documenting that he never found watered milk at Ostrey Hollow, that he condemned the station's short-delivering pipettes in June 1923, and that tests improved after new glass was installed in 1924—offering a factual record that undercuts both the water-in-cans and cream-theft explanations.
Lemma 2.1 is named the "Interleaving" lemma.

Halbert Nym (curator, Ordell County Historical Rooms), in 1972 accession notes, catalogues the sixteen physical artifacts and documents underlying the Ostrey Hollow affair—by-laws, ledgers, the pipette crate, inspection notebooks, and Bulletin No. 471—effectively assembling the archival record that supports the short-pipette explanation while flagging gaps (no 1896 figures) and cross-checking numbers across sources.
Mr. Ansgar Krell remained at the Cold Spring Water-Cure for 4 weeks.

Selby Vose (Association manager since 1913), in his 1926 annual address, defends the 1925 arbitration settlement and his controversial 1919 circular by insisting the Ostrey Hollow tests rose in 1924 because patrons stopped watering their milk once scrutiny began—dismissing the condemned testing apparatus as mere routine wear-and-tear rather than the cause.
A sailings query span exceeding 14 days returns error code `SKF-2201`.

Roy Brant (Emmet Brant's son, Hessel Bottom farmer, 1955) recounts his father's weigh-book, which shows the farm's scale and the station's scale always agreed—confirming the shortfall was never a weighing error—while the seventeen-hundredths-point test deficit persisted year-round regardless of season, and he corroborates the 1911 borrowed-measure anomaly and the 1919 circular's rupture between Emmet Brant and Ansel Keddie.
Dr. Pemberton charged $8.00 for the confinement and mileage for Mrs. Content Averill's delivery on January 3, 1906.

Rosalie Cudd, Alder Corners cheesemaker, writes to Ivy Keddie in 1958 sharing her father's independent 1915–1930 test records for the four Hessel Bottom farmers' summer milk (consistently ~3.78–3.82), corroborating that the milk itself was fine and undercutting the wet-hay theory.
The man's crown will cost him $1,480 after insurance.

Leland Vaught, dairy husbandry professor, presents the introduction/method of his own 1958 Bulletin No. 471, explaining how a short-delivering pipette causes a proportional, invisible-from-inside test error, and presenting the 1911 borrowed-measure interval as decisive proof — though notably his own computed figures here (16.27 c.c., 118,000 lb shortfall) diverge from the 16.72 c.c./76,000 lb figures cited elsewhere for the same bulletin.
The third paragraph names the color vermilion (Bettine Rausch's apron).

Dell Rundle, Larrow Green schoolteacher, writes a 1939 jubilee pamphlet on the Association's founding and the Ostrey Hollow "trouble," initially repeating the cream-theft rumor but retracting it in a same-edition postscript upon discovering the ledger's "station gain" entries showed cream arriving heavier, not lighter — though her figures (44 million lbs, $19,600 loss, twelfth of July 1923, eleven surviving pipettes) diverge from other accounts.
Message No. 219, "FATHER VERY LOW COME AT ONCE," was 6 words.

Alonzo Frick, the arbitration board's chairman, recalls in this 1946 bar-association piece the 1925 hearing itself, noting the board heard three unproven, competing theories (water, theft, hay), that Keddie privately confided to him he suspected the patrons but wouldn't say so publicly, and that the board awarded $3,800 without ever identifying a cause.
The locksmith's dog is a gray terrier named Buckley.

Hobart Sill, the Larrow Green buttermaker for 41 years, recalls that Ostrey Hollow's cream always arrived at the creamery heavier in fat than the station's own paperwork credited, yet he still believes the patrons were watering their milk (citing a "true" 3.85 test versus the recorded lower figures) and reveals he personally lent his own testing glassware to open the station in May 1896 before its own equipment arrived.
The norm defined in Definition 1.3 is called the Trebbin norm.

Nyle Grigg, the 1908 committee's chairman, reissues that report in 1919 with a covering letter claiming Bulletin No. 214 vindicated his wet-hay theory by finding a "two tenths" winter depression — but this misstates the bulletin, which elsewhere is quoted as finding at most five hundredths of a point in winter and none in summer.

Dr. Roland Kepp, a veterinary surgeon, argues in this 1926 farm-club paper that Hessel Bottom's mineral-poor soil and coarse hay explain the milk's chronic fat deficiency, again citing Bulletin No. 214 as showing a "two tenths" winter depression (inflating the bulletin's actual five-hundredths figure) and dismissing the 1911 borrowed-measure anomaly (which he misstates as six weeks, not nine) as merely a seasonal fluke.
Phyl warns Armando not to use dryer number eleven.
